USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the Osaka pause and press talks without new U.S. commitments or new tariffs. Do not roll back List 1–3 or take Huawei off the Entity List until China delivers verifiable farm purchases and puts structural IP/enforcement language back on the table. License non-sensitive U.S. component sales to Huawei case-by-case so chip suppliers are not collateral damage, but keep the Entity List and the unused ~$300B tariff threat as leverage. If Beijing continues to deny the farm pledge and treats existing U.S. tariffs as the only issue, hold the current tariff stock rather than conceding first.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly elevated, not existential. Combined Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B and List 3 is at 25% (timeline 2018-09-24, 2019-05-10); China has matched on ~$60B and raised those rates after May 13. That retaliation is biting a key U.S. export sector: soybean exports to China plunged on the order of 74% by volume, total U.S. soy exports were down ~25%, and USDA authorized up to $16B in farmer aid on 2019-05-23 because China, once the top soy customer, shifted to Brazil. Markets are pricing a growth headwind: the 10-year yield fell from 2.74% (2019-01-22) to 2.06% (2019-07-17), and the Fed’s July 5 Monetary Policy Report attributed the decline to trade tensions and a weaker global outlook. Huawei listing (2019-05-16) plus Google/chip-supplier cutoffs also hit U.S. vendors, which is why Trump offered limited sales relief at Osaka. This is not a clear U.S. opportunity either: May 5–10 showed Beijing can walk back a near-finished text, and mid-July reporting says China denies an unconditional farm-purchase pledge, USDA weekly data showed soy buys slowing after Osaka, and Lighthizer/Mnuchin–Liu He contact on July 9 restarted talks with the same gaps (legal changes, enforcement, subsidies) that blew up in May. Escalating now (List 4 / harder Huawei cutoff) would likely trigger more farm and rare-earth/unreliable-entity retaliation and put consumer goods in the tariff net, which is why Osaka held new tariffs “for the time being.” Full or partial rollback would surrender the only working leverage after the May renegotiation. Negotiate—without new U.S. giveaways—is the stance that matches a +0.22 threat: costly enough to need a channel, not dangerous enough to pay for a pause China is already pocketing.
key_factors: Osaka truce paused the ~$300B List 4 threat but left existing ~$250B/25% tariffs in place
May collapse after China walked back structural/legal text; July 9 call restarted talks with the same core gaps
U.S. farm-belt exposure: soy-to-China collapse, $16B USDA aid, post-Osaka purchases not materializing
Huawei Entity List still in force (presumption of denial); only limited, contested license relief after Osaka
10-year yield down ~68 bp; Fed July MPR cites trade tensions as a growth/financial-conditions headwind

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets negotiations going too slowly and China attempting to renegotiate; orders List 3 to 25% on May 10 and preparation of tariffs on remaining ~$300B.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List.
G20 Osaka: resume talks; existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs for the time being; Trump says he will ease some Huawei restrictions while Huawei remains on the Entity List.
U.S. 10-year yield latest 2.06% on 2019-07-17, change -0.68 (-24.8%) over the window.
China denies an explicit Osaka farm-purchase commitment; USDA data show soy buys slowed after the meeting (127,800 tons, down 79% week-over-week).
USDA authorized up to $16 billion in programs aligned with estimated impacts of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agriculture.
Talks relaunch after Osaka with little sign differences have narrowed; sources say China made no firm immediate ag-purchase commitment.
July 5, 2019 MPR: Treasury yields moved significantly lower over H1 2019, largely reflecting concerns about trade tensions and the global outlook.
As of mid-July, BIS had not removed Huawei from the Entity List; July 1 staff email kept the presumption-of-denial license policy.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep talking on the Osaka ceasefire without new purchase, legal-change, or tariff-rollback commitments. Leave June retaliatory tariffs in place as leverage, and do not launch a fresh tariff, rare-earth, or unreliable-entity shock while Washington’s ~$300B tranche is paused. Treat any farm buys or Huawei relief as items to be exchanged against written, matching U.S. moves—not as prepayments to restart talks.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. After the May collapse, List 3 is at 25% on ~$200B and combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is ~$250B (timeline 2019-05-10 / 2018-09-24); Huawei and affiliates were added to the Entity List on 16 May, with Google and major U.S. chip suppliers pausing sales (2019-05-16 / 2019-05-20). That pairing hits both the export machine and the national-champion tech path. Fresh official data show Q2 GDP at 6.2%—the slowest since 1992—June exports −1.3% and imports −7.3%, and the statistics spokesman calling conditions “still severe both at home and abroad.” That sits near the CHN +0.5 anchor (major export hit + firm-level Huawei targeting) but below it: growth is still inside the 6–6.5% target, June industrial production (+6.3%) and retail sales (+9.8%) held up, H1 trade with the U.S. still produced a larger surplus as China cut U.S. imports far more than the reverse, and the 29 June Osaka deal stopped the next ~$300B hike “for the time being.” Escalating now would likely invite that tranche and deepen the slowdown; conceding purchases or structural legal changes while Huawei remains listed (Temporary General License only through 19 August; Commerce still treating it as blacklisted) and existing tariffs stay at 25% would spend leverage for atmospherics. The 9 July Liu He–Lighthizer–Mnuchin call was only “constructive,” sources say the May text gap on sovereignty/law changes is unbridged, and China has not actually locked in the farm purchases Trump claimed. Action score 0 / negotiate is therefore the stance that matches a serious but manageable threat: use the ceasefire, do not widen it, and do not pay up front.
key_factors: List 3 at 25% and ~$250B of Chinese exports still under Section 301; ~$300B next tranche paused only at Osaka
Huawei Entity List plus chip/Android cutoff is a structural tech hit; TGL expires 19 Aug and delisting has not happened
Q2 GDP 6.2% (27-year low), June exports -1.3%, but IP/retail and the official growth band are holding
Talks restarted 9 July with no text, no matching U.S. rollback, and disputed farm-purchase claims
Further Chinese escalation risks reopening List 4; unilateral concessions would spend leverage before any U.S. move

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
G20 Osaka: Trump and Xi agree to resume talks. Existing tariffs remain; no new tariffs for the time being. Trump says he will ease some Huawei restrictions (Huawei remains on the Entity List).
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (higher rates phased in; many effective June 1).
Chinese officials said the economy grew 6.2 percent between April and June... the slowest pace in China since... 1992. Exports dipped 1.3 percent in June... imports fell 7.3 percent.
U.S. and Chinese trade officials held a constructive phone conversation on Tuesday... There are no miracles here.
Three sources... say that the Chinese side did not make firm commitments to immediately purchase agricultural commodities... Huawei [still] treated as a blacklisted entity.
No official action by BIS regarding removing Huawei from the Entity List... Temporary General License... until Aug. 19, 2019.
U.S. 10-year yield 2.06% on 2019-07-17, down ~68 bp (~25%) over the window—market pricing of slower growth / trade-war risk.
